lignes.texte: The man who volunteered to go into a Nazi death camp… the women who built a bomb one pinch of
gunpowder at a time….and the children who played in a swimming pool feet away from gas chambers.
Here are 50 insane facts about Auschwitz.
When most people picture Auschwitz, they imagine a single fence and a
set of iron-wrought gates with the words Arbeit Macht Frei, or “Work Makes You Free.”
The reality was far more terrifying.
Auschwitz was actually a massive complex of over 40 concentration and extermination
subcamps spread across occupied Poland. The three main sites covered dozens of square miles. There
was Auschwitz I, the original camp; Auschwitz II-Birkenau, the industrial killing center; and
Auschwitz III-Monowitz, the slave labor compound. That’s before you count the satellite camps hidden
inside coal mines, chemical plants, farms, and weapons factories scattered across Upper Silesia.
The Nazi infrastructure for mass murder took a lot of planning,
and its scale is almost impossible to fathom.
Between 1940 and 1945, approximately 1.3 million
people were deported to Auschwitz. About 1.1 million of them were murdered.
That’s the same as killing 220 people a day for 5 straight years.
Put another way, if you counted one victim per second without stopping,
it would take nearly 13 full days, day and night, with no breaks to count
them all. Most of the victims were never registered. They just stepped off a train,
walked a few hundred yards, and were reduced to ashes within the hour.
For most of them, the camp that killed them wasn’t even the original one.
Auschwitz II-Birkenau, the extermination camp, was built specifically to be as
large and spacious as possible. Constructed on drained marshland,
it spanned over 340 acres (138 hectares) and eventually contained more than 300 barracks.
Its designers built a factory for death with an internal railway line running directly to
the gas chambers.. Capable of running around the clock, it became tragically efficient.
Yet when Auschwitz opened, not a single prisoner was Jewish.
When the camp opened in June 1940, the first 728 prisoners were Polish political
detainees. Intellectuals, resistance members, and priests all transported from a prison in Tarnow.
Auschwitz was built to crush the Polish resistance. The mass murder of Jewish
people in the gas chambers didn’t begin until 1942, meaning the camp
was a ruthless killing machine long before the Final Solution ever arrived at its gates.
Zyklon B, the chemical that killed over a million people, started life as a commercial pesticide.
Sold legally as an insecticide for fumigating ships, warehouses,
and clothing, Auschwitz was using it to delouse prisoners. Then SS officer Karl Fritzsch,
the camp's deputy commandant had a monstrous idea.
Fritzsch acted while Camp Commandant Rudolf Höss was away. The decision
that defined the Holocaust's killing method was made by a deputy on his own initiative.
When Fritzsch greeted Auschwitz's first transport. Addressing the initial 728 Polish prisoners in
June 1940, he told them: "You came here not to a sanatorium, but to a German concentration camp,
from which there is no other way out but through the chimney… If there are Jews in the transport,
they have the right to live no longer than two weeks… the rest three months."
That Christmas, he had placed the bodies of prisoners who
had frozen to death at roll call beneath the camp's Christmas tree.
But Fritzsch had already shown his dark side…
Six weeks before Fritzsch's Zyklon B experiment, the basement of Block
11 had been the site of another atrocity. On July 29th, 1941, a headcount found three
prisoners missing. So Fritzsch sentenced 10 random men to starve to death in an underground cell.
One of the condemned, a Polish sergeant named Franciszek Gajowniczek, screamed for his wife and
children. A Franciscan priest Maximilian Kolbe stepped forward and offered to take his place.
After 16 days, Kolbe and three others were still alive. The SS killed them with lethal injection.
Six weeks later, Fritzsch returned to the same basement with 600 Soviet prisoners
of war and 250 sick inmates. He dropped Zyklon B through the vents, but because
cells weren't airtight, the gas dispersed unevenly. The dying was agonizingly slow.
SS personnel returned the following morning to find survivors still alive,
and administered a second dose to finish the job. The basement of
Block 11 had just become the world's first operational gas chamber. Within months,
purpose-built killing wings were under construction.
The industrialization of mass murder had officially begun.
Most Nazi camps used paper records for their prisoners. Auschwitz used flesh.
Starting in 1942, every prisoner received a number tattooed directly onto their left forearm.
Over 400,000 people were branded this way. Jewish prisoners arriving after
May 1944 were given an "A" or "B" tattoo. Roma prisoners got a "Z."
For those who survived the horrors, that ink became a permanent scar. A
lifelong reminder of what had been done to them.
But of all the symbols at Auschwitz,
the most famous one contains a secret most people don’t know about.
“ARBEIT MACHT FREI”... work sets you free.
The infamous sign above Auschwitz was forged by Polish prisoner blacksmiths under orders from the
SS. But the prisoners, led by Jan Liwacz, were determined to leave their own mark.
The men turned the letter “B” in ARBEIT upside down as a literal
middle finger to the Nazis. The SS, never noticed.
The upside-down B has remained one of the most enduring symbols of resistance in the
camp’s history. And it wasn't the only time someone would mess with the sign.
In December 2009, staff at the Auschwitz Museum made a shocking discovery.
The original gate, complete with its 95-pound (43 kg) iron sign,
was gone. Thieves had broken in under the cover of darkness and unscrewed it
from its hinges. A manhunt was launched across Poland. 3 days later, police found the sign,
cut into three pieces, hidden in a forest in the north of the country.
The mastermind was a Swedish neo-Nazi named Anders Högestrom,
who was later sentenced to almost 3 years in prison. The original sign sits
inside the museum for safekeeping, while a replica hangs on the gate.
The Nazis designed a diet meant to work prisoners to death.
Inmates were given a meager 700 calories per day while performing
brutal physical labor. That’s less than a third of what a typical adult needs.
A typical day's rations could be a bitter cup of coffee in the morning.
Lunch was a watery bowl of soup made from rotting vegetables or scraps of
meal. Dinner was a small crust of bread with a scrape of margarine at night.
On this diet, the average prisoner's life expectancy was a matter of weeks.
And if the food didn’t break you, the weather would finish the job.
Twice a day, prisoners faced a living nightmare known as Appell,
the mandatory roll call. It was weaponized psychological torture disguised as beaurocracy.
Beginning at 4 a.m., thousands of prisoners in thin striped uniforms were
forced to stand in the freezing Polish winter. If the numbers didn’t add up,
the entire camp stood there until it was resolved. It could last for hours.
Anyone who collapsed from the cold or exhaustion was mercilessly beaten.
And if a prisoner died during roll call? Their bodies were propped up and counted all the same.
Despite everything, a shadow economy operated inside Auschwitz.
Prisoners inside the camp would trade bread, cigarettes, margarine, and medicine as an illegal,
informal currency. Survival could depend on the inmate's work assignment. Those lucky
enough to work in the warehouses could smuggle out extra food and valuables.
For many prisoners, learning to navigate the underground was just as important as
any other skill. And the center of it all, was a warehouse complex with the most unlikely name.
Prisoners called the massive complex where victims’ confiscated belongings were Kanada.
Eastern European Jews associated Canada with wealth, abundance, and a land of plenty. And
Kanada was, by Auschwitz standards, obscenely abundant. 30 barracks stuffed floor to ceiling
with items like clothing, jewelry, food, medicine, money, and children’s toys.
Every item belonged to the thousands who arrived at the camp on trains. The
Nazis sorted it all and shipped it back to Germany for redistribution
to civilian families. Working here was the most coveted assignment in the camp.
It was the one place that could keep you alive.
On January 27th, 1945, Soviet troops marched into Auschwitz… and openly wept.
The Nazis had fled in such a panic, they had left behind the staggering evidence of their crimes.
Inside the camp’s warehouses, soldiers found hundreds of thousands of clothes,
shoes and eyeglasses. Alongside those items, was something even more disturbing. Thousands of
pounds of human hair, shaved from prisoners before they were gassed. The hair was packed into bales,
ready to be shipped back to Germany, where it would be used to make felt, rope, and fabric.
Most haunting of all were the hundreds of prosthetic limbs
stacked in piles like lumber. They belonged to the disabled victims who
were taken to the gas chambers the moment they stepped off the trains.
The Soviets had walked into one of the greatest crime scenes in human history.
Between May and July of 1944, 420,000 Hungarian Jews were deported to Auschwitz.
It was one of the largest national deportations of the entire Holocaust.
Upon arrival, SS doctors would walk the line of exhausted, disoriented prisoners
and flick their finger left or right. Left meant the gas chamber. Right, slave labor.
Roughly 75% or 330,000 people were sent left. They
were gassed and cremated without ever being registered as prisoners.
By late July 1944, nearly the entire Jewish
population outside of Budapest had been eradicated or removed.
SS doctor Josef Mengele is the man most associated with the selection processes.
But any SS doctor on duty could perform the tasks. For many of them,
it was just part of the morning routine.
Mengele would arrive on the ramp immaculately dressed,
sometimes whistling opera as he worked. With a flick of his hand,
he sent thousands of people to their deaths. Children under 14, the elderly, pregnant women,
and mothers with young children almost always went left. They were dead before the day was over.
At the absolute peak of those deportations,
the pace of what came next was something almost indescribable.
At its peak, trains were arriving at Auschwitz around the clock,
unloading thousands of people at a time. The SS scaled up the operation
until they were processing and murdering around 12,000 people every single day.
A life was ending every 7 seconds.
The system became so efficient, the crematoria couldn't keep up. Those
too sick or frail to walk were loaded onto trucks. Everyone else marched.
They were told they were being taken to the camp, but had to undergo disinfection
first. They were forced to strip outside before being herded through the doors.
And one they slammed shut, the living nightmare intensified.
Auschwitz Birkenau had 4 massive crematoria complexes with a
combined capacity of over 4,000 bodies per day.
But during the peak of the Hungarian deportations, that wasn’t even close to enough to handle
the volume. The SS forced prisoners to dig 6 enormous burning pits right next to Crematorium
V and reopened old pits in the nearby woods. The skies above the camp were filled with
endless smoke, but burning alone didn't erase the dead completely. Bones survived the flames.
So the Sonderkommando ground the remaining fragments into powder
using pestles. That powder was dumped into the Soła and Vistula rivers,
scattered across fields as agricultural fertilizer, and used as landfill.
But the stripping of human identity began long before anyone reached the crematorium.
The machinery of deception at Auschwitz-Birkenau was meticulous.
After victims were stripped, they were walked into a large tiled room
fitted with metal showerheads mounted in the ceiling. The doors locked behind them. Then,
through vents above, SS men in gas masks poured in crystallized Zyklon B.
After death, the Sonderkommando dragged out the bodies, cut the women's hair,
extracted all gold dental work and jewelry, and sent the remains to the furnaces. The
fake showerheads were never connected to any plumbing. They existed only to
prevent panic for the 15 minutes or so it took to kill everyone inside.
Incredibly, despite the horrors of Auschwitz, one man decided to voluntarily walk straight into it.
In 1940, Polish resistance fighter Captain Witold
Pilecki was swept up in a street roundup in Warsaw… deliberately.
His mission was to infiltrate the Auschwirtz,
build an underground resistance, and smuggle intelligence reports to the outside world.
And he did exactly that…for 2 and a half years.
He organized a secret prisoner network, sabotaged facilities,
and sent out detailed reports describing the mass murders taking place. His escape
in April 1943, was straight out of a thriller.
He arranged a night shift at the camp bakery around a mile (1.6 km) outside the perimeter
and cut the phone and alarm lines while the guards slept. He then used a bump key
to force the door open, barricaded the SS men inside and slipped into the darkness.
What happened to him after the war is one of the most heartbreaking
twists in this entire story. But the information he provided was vital.
By March 1941, Pilecki's reports of the gas chambers, the daily murders,
and the scale of the operation were being forwarded to the Polish
government-in-exile in London and the British and other Allied governments.
They became the principal source of Western Allied
intelligence on Auschwitz-Birkenau. But Allied leadership dismissed them
as exaggerations. They just could accept that what Pilecki was describing was true.
The inability to act remains one of the most debated moral failures of the Second World War.
But not every intelligence report out of Auschwitz was ignored. Two men who
barely made it out with their lives wrote something that changed history.
On April 7, 1944, Slovak Jewish prisoners Rudolf Vrba and Alfred
Wetzler executed one of the most daring escapes in the history of the Holocaust.
With the help of the camp underground,
they crawled inside a hollowed-out cavity hidden in a wood pile. But they weren’t safe.
To mask their scent from the camp’s 200 trained Alsatian search dogs, they soaked tobacco in
petrol and scattered it around their hiding spot. They stayed there for 3 full days while SS teams
hunted for them. After the search was called off, they slipped out and marched for 11 days
through enemy territory. They covered 80 miles (129 km) in total, eventually reaching Slovakia.
When they arrived, they dictated a 32-page report with detailed maps, gas chamber diagrams,
and an estimated death toll of 1.75 million. The Vrba-Wetzler Report is credited with
helping to prevent the deportation of an additional 200,000 Hungarian Jews.
And the man responsible for the selections that report was trying
to stop? He was still at work on the arrival ramp when Vrba and Wetzler were writing it.
Josef Mengele harbored an obsessive, sadistic fixation on twins, believing
their genetics held the secret to rapidly growing the Aryan race.
Up to 1,500 twins were pulled from the selection line, spared the gas chambers, and sent to
Mengele's special barracks. There, he injected them with unknown substances in attempts to
change their eye color. He deliberately infected them with diseases. And surgical sewed siblings
together to create artificial conjoined twins. Prisoner doctor Miklós Nyiszli later testified
that on one occasion, Mengele personally killed 14 twins in a single night by injecting chloroform
directly into their hearts, just so he could conduct simultaneous autopsies the next morning.
He called the twins his "children." Survivors called him the Angel of Death.
As Nazi Germany collapsed, Mengele slipped through Allied lines on forged papers. He worked as a
farmhand in Bavaria, before fleeing to Argentina in 1949 via the infamous Nazi “ratlines.”
He later moved to Paraguay, then Brazil, where he lived among other
Nazi exiles. Despite being one of the most wanted war criminals in the world,
he was never captured. He drowned after having a stroke while swimming near São Paulo in 1979, at
the age of 67. He was seemingly free, unrepentant, and never spent a single day in a courtroom.
His bones were exhumed and forensically identified in 1985. Sadly, justice never found him.
Rudolf Höss, the man who helped design the gas chambers of Auschwitz,
oversaw the murder of over a million people.
Every night he went home to House Number 88, a comfortable villa that shared a garden
wall with the camp perimeter. The family built gardens, walking paths, a greenhouse, a sauna,
and a swimming pool on site. Hedwig Höss, his wife, called it their family "paradise." There
the Höss children swam, paddled on the river, and adored the man they knew as a loving father.
And to make the commute between that family life and his murderous profession as easy as possible,
Höss had a tunnel built connecting the basement of the villa directly to his office at the camp.
When he was eventually transferred to a desk job in Berlin, Hedwig refused
to leave. She stayed in the house with the children until the end of the war.
At Nuremberg, Rudolf Höss’s testimony was chilling. He spoke about the superiority
of Zyklon B over carbon monoxide, the advantages of Auschwitz over other facilities,
and the screaming that told him when people in the gas chambers had died.
But in the letter he wrote to his wife from his Polish prison cell days before execution,
something changed. He called himself “the greatest destroyer of human beings who
carried out every order to exterminate people no matter what”. In the very same paragraph,
he insisted that he was “by nature gentle, good natured, and very helpful.”
Höss told his wife to change the family name, which had been disgraced and enclosed his
wedding ring. Whether he felt genuine remorse or it was an elaborate excuse remains unknown.
Before he wrote that letter, of course, he had to be found.
After the war, Höss spent almost a year working as a gardener in
Schleswig-Holstein under the name "Franz Lang”.
But somehow, a German-Jewish Nazi hunter named Hanns Alexander tracked him down.
Höss denied everything, but Alexander noticed his wedding ring,
and threatened to cut off his finger if he didn't remove it. Engraved inside was
Höss's real name. As soldiers confirmed the identification,
they beat Höss with axe handles. He also tried to bite down on a cyanide capsule. Neither worked.
At Nuremberg, he testified that he had personally overseen the deaths of at least
2.5 million people. On April 16th, 1947, a gallows was built directly beside the
gas chamber and crematorium at Auschwitz I and, fittingly, he was hanged there.
But Höss's capture and execution was the exception
Over the course of Auschwitz’s operation,
approximately 7,000-8,000 SS men and over 200 female guards served within the camp complex.
After the war, around 673 SS personnel from Auschwitz were brought to trial. The rest
melted back into ordinary postwar German society. They became teachers, policemen,
and businessmen, raised families, drew pensions, and died of old age. Historians have called
this one of the great scandals of postwar history, and it's hard to argue with them.
The horrors of Auschwitz weren’t just funded
by ideology. They were also propped up by corporate greed.
German companies, including a few you probably know, literally paid for slave labor at Auschwitz.
The main culprit was IG Farben, a massive German chemical conglomerate
whose divisions include household names like BASF and Bayer. The corporation
built a massive synthetic rubber and oil plant right next to Auschwitz.
Just to exploit prisoner slave labor.
IG Farben paid the SS a daily rate in exchange for a supply of workers,
with the price varying depending on their skills or age. When prisoners became too weak to work,
IG Farben returned them to the SS, who gassed them. By 1943, almost half of IG
Farben's 330,000-strong workforce consisted of slave laborers and conscripts including
30,000 Auschwitz prisoners. Over 25,000 people died on the plant’s construction site alone.
But the company's pharmaceutical division,
which eventually became Bayer, went further than just exploiting free labor.
Helmuth Vetter, an Auschwitz camp physician, SS captain,
and Bayer employee, conducted drug experiments on inmates.
In one study, Bayer paid 170 reichsmarks per person for 150 female prisoners to
test an anesthetic. A Bayer employee wrote to Commandant Höss: "The… women arrived in
good condition. However, we were unable to obtain conclusive results because they died during the
experiments. We would kindly request that you send us another group of women… at the same price."
Bayer also provided the chemicals and disease agents used in Mengele's twin experiments. Eva
Mozes Kor and her twin sister Miriam were among those subjected to experiments. Miriam's kidneys
were permanently damaged and never grew to normal adult size. She died of kidney disease in 1993.
Bayer continued operating after the war and today generates tens
of billions of dollars in annual revenue.
The Sonderkommando units at Auschwitz operated under a policy of scheduled
extinction. After 3 or 4 months of labor, the SS would kill the entire unit and replace them
with new arrivals. Knowing the end was coming, the 12th Sonderkommando,
the group operating in 1944, decided to strike back. A group of Jewish women
working in a camp munitions factory began smuggling in the only thing they could.
Gunpowder.
Led by 21 year old Roza Robota, the women smuggled tiny amounts of gunpowder inside their uniforms.
They passed the packages to male prisoners who hid them under corpses during transport. After a
long and agonizing 18 months, they had enough to fill sardine tins and make crude bombs.
They knew that if they were ever discovered, it would mean immediate death. They did it anyway.
Then came the day the Sonderkommando used them.
On October 7, 1944, the 12th Sonderkommando received word
that the SS had come to execute them. Instead, they revolted.
Prisoners detonated the sardine tin bombs at Crematorium IV,
and tore the building apart with axes, hammers, and knives. At Crematorium II,
prisoners sliced through the electrified perimeter fence and ran.
The SS response was merciless.
Guards mounted machine guns on rooftops and fired blindly through the ceilings into the
barracks below. At the ruins of Crematorium IV, approximately 200 prisoners were forced to lie
face down in the dirt and were shot one by one in the back of the head. Locals helped the Nazis
hunt down the escapees. 450 prisoners were killed that day. But Crematorium IV never operated again.
When the SS went looking for the women who had made it possible, they found 4 of them.
What those women did next belongs in a different category of courage entirely.
Desperate to uncover the ringleaders, the Nazis tortured some of the male Sonderkommando
prisoners. Eventually broke and gave up the names of the women who had smuggled them the gunpowder.
When Roza Robota, Ella Gaertner, Estera Wajcblum, and Regina Safirsztajn were
arrested and tortured for months, not one of them gave up a single name. Roza,
writing from her cell, passed a friend a note signed “be strong and of good courage.”
On January 5th, 1945, four gallows were erected in the women's camp. The assembled
prisoners were forced to watch as Roza Robota sang defiantly before the trapdoor opened.
Before they were led to their death, some prisoners composed detailed accounts of
everything they had seen. They buried them in the ground near the crematoria.
Between 1945 and 1980, 8 separate caches of manuscripts were discovered,
mostly by accident. One manuscript spoke of “suffering the human mind
cannot imagine” and the casual doling out of death where humans were reduced to ash.
Auschwitz operated six separate prisoner orchestras. Every morning and evening, musicians
were forced to stand at the gates and play military marches as work columns shuffled past.
The Woman’s Orchestra, led by Alma Rosé,
was a 40-to-50-piece ensemble made up of dozen nationalities. The SS would address
Rosé as "Frau Alma,” a title that was denied to every other Jewish prisoner in Birkenau.
When Rosé died suddenly in April 1944, the SS approved a memorial in her honor. It was
the only time that SS officers formally mourned a Jewish prisoner in a camp.
But what Rosé actually did was far more deliberate than the SS ever realized.
Alma Rosé understood exactly what the orchestra meant to its members. She
never threw anyone out for poor playing; instead she found them
another role. Being removed meant returning to the general population and guaranteed death.
When a violinist contracted typhus and faced selection, Rosé told the SS the woman was one
of her finest players. She negotiated heating for the music block, arguing the instruments
would be ruined by cold. She secured indoor roll calls and a rest period after meals.
Almost all of the Women's Orchestra survived the war. When survivors were
later asked what they thought of Alma Rosé, the answer was "She saved us."
While Rosé's orchestra played,
other prisoners were channeling everything they had into something far more dangerous
Over the course of the camp’s operation, there were at least 802 documented escape
attempts involving 928 prisoners. Around 144 are believed to have succeeded. The punishment
for a failed escape was death by public hanging in front of the other prisoners.
But the retribution didn't stop there. If an escaped prisoner couldn't be found,
10 prisoners chosen at random from the escapee's block were executed. This collective punishment
system created fear and suspicion among the prisoners. Would people risk the
lives of others for self-preservation? It was a form of psychological torture.
Of the roughly 144 prisoners who made it out,
none carried evidence more haunting than one 18 year-old survivor.
In spring 1945, Lilly Jacob was liberated from Mittelbau-Dora concentration camp
and found an album in an abandoned SS barracks. Inside were nearly 200
photographs documenting the arrival and selection of Hungarian Jews at Birkenau.
As Lilly turned the pages, she recognized herself on the arrival ramp,
alongside her brothers and neighbors from her hometown. She never saw any of them again.
The album is the only visual document
of what happened in the first hours after a train arrived at Auschwitz.
Another group suffered a genocide that history has barely begun to acknowledge.
The Nazis deported approximately 23,000 Roma and Sinti people to a
special section of Auschwitz-Birkenau known as the "Gypsy Camp.” Unlike most other prisoners,
Roma families were initially kept together. But on the night of August
2nd, 1944, the SS gassed the 2,900 remaining men, women, and children.
The entire camp was wiped out.
The Roma genocide killed between 500,000 and 1.5 million Roma across occupied
Europe. In , Romani it’s known as the Porajmos, or “the Devouring,”
An equally invisible story belongs to the Soviet prisoners of war who
came to Auschwitz near the very beginning and most never left.
Approximately 15,000 Soviet prisoners of war were
sent to Auschwitz. And nearly all of them died within months of arrival.
The racialized ideology on the Eastern Front meant that Soviet POWs occupied the absolute
lowest rung of the camp's brutal hierarchy. They received the least food, the harshest treatment,
and were used as subjects for some of the earliest systematic killing experiments.
By the end of the war, only a few hundred survived. Their
fate remains one of the least-discussed atrocities within the Auschwitz complex.
Regardless of the group, every prisoner feared being sent to one specific building.
Block 11, known as the “Death Block,” housed an SS
summary court that could sentence prisoners to death on the spot.
It also boasted solitary confinement and standing cells which were stone closets
3 feet by 3 feet (0.9m by 0.9m). 4 prisoners would be crammed into each
cell after laboring all day. They would be left to stand through the night before
being released for another day of work. Some prisoners endured this for weeks.
In the courtyard between Block 10 and Block 11 stood the "Black Wall,"
where an estimated 20,000 people were executed.
Block 11, the standing cells, the Black Wall, all of it was still there when the
Soviets arrived in January 1945. Most of the prisoners, though, were not.
On January 17th, 1945, the SS forced almost 58,000 prisoners onto a march through the Polish winter.
There was little food or winter clothing, as temperatures dipped well below freezing.
Prisoners that fell behind or tried to escape were shot where they stood.
Tens of thousands of people died on those marches. People who had survived months
or years at Auschwitz had their lives taken within walking distance of freedom.
The SS were intent on killing right up until the very end.
When the Soviets arrived 10 days later,
they found a crime scene so enormous the Nazis hadn't come close to covering it up.
As the Nazi war machine crumbled, the SS guards at Auschwitz scrambled to erase
what they had done. Beyond the death marches, they detonated the crematoria
and gas chambers with explosives, and burned tens of thousands of documents.
But the scale of the operation had been too large, too long-running,
and too physical for any cover-up to succeed. The warehouses were still full of stolen goods,
and the camp’s ruins were still standing. Roughly 7,500 prisoners were too sick to
be marched and were still inside the wire when the Soviet 60th Army arrived.
One man had tried to warn the world about all of this years before Soviet soldiers ever reached
the gates. What his own country did to him afterward is almost impossible to believe.
After escaping Auschwitz and telling the world about the horrors, Witold Pilecki
didn’t stop fighting. He continued working as a resistance operative,
this time against the Soviet-backed communist regime that had taken over Poland.
He was arrested by the Polish communist secret police in 1947 and tortured into
signing a false confession. After a show trial, 47 year old Pilecki was executed
with a single bullet to the back of the head on May 25th, 1948. His name was suppressed by
the communist government for decades, but was posthumously rehabilitated in 1990.
He’s now widely regarded as one of Poland's greatest national heroes.
Meanwhile, the legal reckoning for what happened at Auschwitz kept grinding forward,
even decades after the world had moved on.
If you thought the accounting of justice ended in the 1940s, think again. German
courts were still actively prosecuting SS personnel well into the 21st century.
In June 2022, 77 years after the war, a German court sentenced a 101-year-old man to 5 years
in prison for serving as a guard at a camp and aiding in the murder of over 3,500 prisoners.
He had spent the intervening decades as an ordinary civilian. He denied everything.
The case shows how prosecutors are determined that no one escapes justice,
especially those at Auschwitz.
But for the world outside the wire, there was no trial at all.
Auschwitz wasn't some remote, hidden facility tucked away from the world. The town of Oświęcim
sat adjacent to the camp. Residents could see the smoke rising from the crematoria,
smell the burning on the wind, and watch the trains rolling in and out.
The operation ran for 5 years, in plain view, with thousands of SS personnel and
civilian contractors involved. The notion that the surrounding
world didn't know what was happening has been challenged by historians for decades.
The evidence suggests otherwise.
Auschwitz needed hundreds of civilian contractors and suppliers during the construction process.
Among them was Topf & Sons, a German oven manufacturer whose engineers supplied the
crematoria and visited the camp regularly to increase their throughput… at the SS's request.
When one Topf engineer was installing ventilation systems in Crematorium II,
he filed a service report which referred to the room beneath the
building as the “undressing room”. The SS official cover term was the “morgue.”
That single phrase in a routine service document proves he knew
what the space was for. Topf & Sons continued operating after the war.
No one from the company was ever convicted of a crime.
In June 1944, following the publication of the Vrba-Wetzler Report, the BBC broadcast
details of the mass killings at Auschwitz. The New York Times ran stories. The War
Refugee Board in Washington received specific, actionable intelligence including the location
of the rail lines that carried hundreds of thousands of Hungarian Jews to their deaths.
Proposals to bomb those rail lines, or the crematoria themselves,
were considered… and rejected. Military planners argued the raids were not feasible,
or that the military assets were better used elsewhere.
Whether bombing the lines could have saved lives and whether the decision remains a
bitterly contested question in Holocaust history.
What is not contested is that the information was there and ready to be acted upon.
In 2005, the United Nations designated January 27 as International Holocaust Remembrance Day.
The choice was deliberate.
It marks the anniversary of the day in 1945, when Soviet soldiers walked
through the gates of Auschwitz-Birkenau. The camp had become the defining symbol of
the Holocaust. No other location embodied the mechanized scale of the Nazi’s Final Solution.
More than a million stories ended at Auschwitz, and we only know a fraction of them.
For all the statistics, the facts, testimonies and investigations,
the single most important thing about Auschwitz is also the thing hardest to
hold onto. That every single number represents a specific person.
Most of them left no record, because the Nazis didn't bother recording the ones they killed
immediately. They arrived. They were murdered. And the world moved on without knowing their names.
